opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the single most important thing is to just use them a lot, and to use them for things you'd assume they can't do. Most people try a model once or twice, hit some failure, form a mental model like "oh, it hallucinates" or "it's bad at maths," and never update. But the capabilities change every few months, so whatever intuition you formed a year ago is probably out of date.

A practical framing I like: whenever you're about to do a task, take a few seconds and ask, "Could an LLM help with any part of this?" Writing, debugging, summarizing a paper, brainstorming, giving feedback on a draft, explaining some concept you're confused about. Often the answer is yes, and the cost of trying is tiny. If it fails, you've lost thirty seconds and learned something about where the frontier is.

The second thing is that *how* you use them matters enormously. A lot of people write a one-line prompt and judge the model on that. But these systems respond to context the way a smart new colleague would. If you give them background, explain what you're actually trying to achieve, show examples of what good looks like, and tell them what you don't want, the output quality goes way up. I often just dump in a huge amount of context, like a rambling voice memo of everything relevant, and that works surprisingly well.

Third, treat it as a conversation, not a vending machine. Push back. Ask it to critique its own answer. Ask for five options rather than one. Ask, "What would a skeptical expert say about this?" Iterating is where a lot of the value is.

And finally, keep your critical faculties on. They're very capable, but they can be confidently wrong, and they can be sycophantic: they'll tell you your idea is great. So I'd lean on them most where checking is cheap, like code you can run or writing you can read, and be more careful with factual claims you can't verify. But the overall message is that people are underusing them far more often than overusing them, so experiment aggressively.

r001.rationale: The response says capabilities change every few months, old intuitions become outdated, and failed attempts still teach you where the frontier is.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking for critique and a skeptical expert’s view, but does not clearly recommend asking the model to identify blind spots in your knowledge or plans.

r003.rationale: It recommends using LLMs for tasks you would assume they cannot do and trying them even if they might fail.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the single biggest mistake people make is that they tried ChatGPT once in 2023, it was kind of mediocre, and they formed an opinion and never updated it. The models have gotten dramatically better since then, and if your mental model is stuck a few years back, you're just leaving an enormous amount of value on the table.

So my first piece of advice is: use the frontier model. Pay the twenty dollars a month. The free tiers are often noticeably worse, and the gap between the best model and a mediocre one is the gap between "this is a toy" and "this is genuinely useful for my work."

The second thing is to be curious and run lots of cheap experiments. Treat it like learning a new tool rather than asking "can it do my job, yes or no." Just try it on things. Whenever you're about to do something slightly tedious, or you're stuck, or you have a question you'd normally Google, throw it at the model and see what happens. The cost of a failed experiment is thirty seconds. The cost of never discovering that it could have saved you an hour a day is enormous.

And you'll quickly build intuition for where the jagged frontier is. These things are weirdly good at some stuff and weirdly bad at other stuff, and the only way to learn the shape of that is to poke at it yourself. For me, the stuff that's been transformative is coding, obviously, but also things like: explaining a paper in a field I don't know, rubber-ducking an idea, drafting the boring first version of an email or doc, or asking "what am I missing here?" about a plan.

The third thing is to give it more context than feels natural. People type one line into the box and get a generic answer and conclude the model is dumb. But if you paste in the whole document, explain what you're actually trying to do and why, and say what you've already tried, you get something dramatically better. The model can't read your mind. A lot of what looks like model stupidity is actually just underspecified prompting.

And relatedly, push back on it. If the answer's wrong or vague, say so and ask again. Have a conversation. Ask it to critique its own answer. It's surprisingly good at that. People treat the first response as the final verdict, when really it's the opening of a dialogue.

Then the last thing I'd say is: stay a bit calibrated about the failure modes. It will confidently make things up sometimes. So for anything where being wrong actually matters, verify it, and lean on it harder for things where you can check the output cheaply or where a mediocre draft is still way better than a blank page. But honestly, I think most people are far too far on the "I don't trust it, I won't use it" end of the spectrum rather than the "I trust it too much" end. And the right thing to do is just use it a lot and let your trust get calibrated by experience.

r001.rationale: The response says models have improved dramatically and recommends cheap experiments to discover what they can do, linking rapid capability changes to the value of trying them.

r002.rationale: It recommends asking, “what am I missing here?” about a plan.

r003.rationale: It advises trying the model when stuck and experimenting rather than deciding in advance whether it can do a task, which supports asking it to tackle problems whose solvability is uncertain.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest thing is to actually try them on things you care about. It’s easy to ask a model a couple of trivia questions, notice a mistake, and conclude that it’s not very useful. But that doesn’t tell you much about whether it could help you with your work.

A habit I’d encourage is: whenever you’re doing something at a computer, pause and ask, “Could an LLM help with this?” Maybe you’re trying to understand a paper, write a difficult email, debug some code, or work out why you’re stuck on a decision. Give it enough context to make a serious attempt.

And then iterate. If the answer is vague, tell it what’s missing. If you don’t understand something, ask it to explain the specific step you’re confused by. You can say, “Ask me questions before answering,” which can be useful when you don’t yet know how to articulate what you need.

You still need to check things, particularly when being wrong matters. But I think there’s a lot to discover by treating it as an interactive tool and experimenting, rather than expecting one prompt to tell you what it’s capable of.

r001.rationale: The response encourages experimentation but does not connect its value to rapid changes in LLM capabilities.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking the model to ask questions, but does not recommend using it to identify blind spots in one's knowledge or plans.

r003.rationale: It recommends trying LLMs on useful tasks, but does not specifically say to ask them to solve problems whose solvability is uncertain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is to actually try them on things you care about. It’s easy to ask a chatbot a couple of trivia questions, notice it makes a mistake, and conclude that it’s not very useful. But that doesn’t tell you much about whether it can help with your work.

Pick a task you’re doing anyway. Maybe you’re trying to understand a paper, write some code, or work through a decision. Give it the context, explain what you’re stuck on, and have a conversation. If the first answer isn’t useful, tell it why. Ask it to take a different approach, or ask you questions before answering.

And try tasks where you can judge the result. If you know some programming, you can check whether the code works. If you’re learning something, you can ask for examples and test whether the explanation makes sense. That lets you develop a feel for where it helps and where you need to be sceptical.

I’d treat this as exploration: spend a bit of time trying it across quite different parts of your life. The useful question is, ‘Can I find ways of using this that make things easier or help me think better?’ You learn that much more effectively through experimenting than through reading someone else’s verdict.

r001.rationale: The response encourages experimentation, but does not say that rapid changes in LLM capabilities make it especially valuable.

r002.rationale: It suggests asking the LLM to ask questions, but does not recommend asking it to identify blind spots in knowledge or plans.

r003.rationale: It recommends trying tasks such as understanding a paper or working through a decision, but does not specifically recommend asking the LLM to solve a problem whose solvability is uncertain.
